changes.text: Entry, stop and target now carry their prices as labels on the price axis, each in its own colour - which is where you look for a price anyway, and the one place a level can be shown without covering a candle. They follow a level while it is being dragged

The tags on the position say what a level is worth rather than repeating what it is: what the stop costs and what the target pays, both in $ and in R. The stop reads −1.00R because that is what R is - the distance to it - and it is the scale the other two numbers are read against

Direction, size and open result sit together in one tag on the entry line - L or S rather than a spelled-out LONG, with the size rounded to something readable instead of eight decimal places. Nothing is left on the block itself but the marker at the entry, so the candles the position is judged against stay clear
The release notes scroll again. Past a screenful of entries the list ran off the bottom of the window with no way to reach the rest

A quick trade bar in the top left of the chart while a replay runs: Buy, a size, Sell. One click sends a market order with no stop and no target - those go on afterwards, by dragging them off the position line. The size field starts empty and both buttons stay off until you set one, because a size left over from a setup that is already over is the one mistake here that costs money

A market order is now on the chart from the moment you send it. It has no price of its own until the next bar answers it, so until now pressing Buy looked like it had done nothing at all - it is drawn dashed at the last close, with its direction and the bar it is waiting for. It still fills on the next bar, at the same costs as everything else
An × at the right end of the position line closes it at market, without going to the panel. It fills on release over the button, so sliding off takes the click back

Stops and targets can be put on a position that has none by dragging off its entry line. Which one you get is decided by where you let go relative to the last price - below the market protects a long and takes profit on a short - not by which way you dragged from the entry

The open position reads at a glance: its zones fade from the level towards the entry so the candles stay clear, a triangle marks where it was opened, and its direction, size and price sit on plates that candles cannot swallow. Long and short take the chart's own up and down colours rather than green and red, which here mean profit and loss and nothing else

Everything the position says is set in the app's text face at a readable size, on rounded chips that match the buttons, and every amount of money now carries a $ - so a tag that shows a level and what being wrong there costs no longer reads as two numbers of unknown kind

A Replay tab that steps through history one bar at a time and lets you trade it by hand. Pick a date and a starting balance; space plays and pauses, the right arrow takes one bar, and anything after the playhead does not exist for the session - the indicators only ever see the bars that have been revealed

Your orders go through the same engine a backtest does: they fill on the bar after the one you are looking at, at the same spread, slippage and commission, and a bar that touched both your stop and your target is decided by walking the minutes inside it. The size follows from your risk and your stop, exactly as it does for a strategy, so a trade taken by hand and one taken by a bot are the same size

Draw the trade and send it. Pull entry, stop and target with the position tool, right-click the block, and it becomes an order - either waiting on the drawn entry, or at market now with the drawn distances measured from the actual fill. Your drawing is replaced by the live position the moment the entry fills

The open position sits on the chart with what it is worth right now against the right edge, in R where there is a stop to measure against. Its stop and target can be dragged straight on the chart - the drag is a preview, and only letting go replaces the protection. A level dropped on the wrong side of the last price is refused, because it would close the position at market rather than protect it

The chart no longer jumps when a bar is revealed. Set the zoom and put the newest candle where you want it, and Step and Play leave it exactly there; scroll back into history and it stays on the bars you are reading
Save session stores a replay as a run in the same library the backtests land in, so an afternoon traded by hand can be put next to what a strategy did over the same bars

Compare runs in the Results tab: ctrl-click several and their curves are laid over one timeline as a percentage of each starting balance - by calendar, or with their starts aligned when they come from different periods. Equity or drawdown, with a readout under the pointer, the metrics side by side with the best cell in each row marked, and a settings diff showing only what actually differs

A gap tool on the drawing toolbar: click an imbalance and it is marked, drawn the way the indicator draws one. A run of stacked gaps can be read as the single zone it is - set how wide a traded strip may be before it counts as a real separation, and neighbouring gaps below that merge into one
Line width and dash are now per drawing, chosen once and kept for the next one you draw

A Ranges indicator that marks the stretches where the market stops going anywhere - and marks them to fit the chart you are on. An hourly range does not appear on a 1m chart. Instead of a fixed percent span, which marks 77% of a 1m chart and nothing at all on 1h, the height is measured against how far this market normally travels in the same number of bars, so one setting means the same thing everywhere

A range has to be reached at both edges more than once, so a narrow diagonal drift no longer counts as one, and it ends on the bar that closes beyond an edge - a wick through the edge only widens it, the way a raid on a level should. The breakout is drawn with its direction, and the equilibrium line down the middle is there for premium and discount

Every part of the definition is a setting with its own explanation: how long, how tight, how many touches per side, how close to an edge counts, and how far past it a close has to be. A range still running at the right edge keeps its levels drawn dashed to the edge of the chart

An Auto backtest tab that tries a whole range of settings at once. Switch any number from Fixed to Range, give it a from, a to and a step, and every combination is run and ranked - the best four against the worst four, because the gap between the two ends is what says whether the setting mattered at all

Every sweep holds part of the range back. The combinations are ranked on the earlier stretch and the ones shown are re-run on the later one, which had no say in choosing them. Where the two numbers disagree the first was noise - trying hundreds of settings on one stretch of history reliably finds the one that memorised it

Any result can be sent straight to the Backtest tab with its market, its range and every setting filled in, so a promising combination gets a full report with its trades to step through. The sweep is the search; the backtest is the reckoning
Sweeps run on their own thread with a progress bar, an estimate of the time left, and a stop button that works between combinations. The app stays usable while one runs, however long it takes

A sweep reuses what it can. Settings that only change what is done with a signal - risk, reward-to-risk, leverage - do not need the signals found again, so the panel shows how many detections a sweep really needs beside how many runs. Trying 17 gap sizes against 19 reward levels on a year of 5-minute bars takes 23 seconds rather than ten minutes

Strategies are their own thing now, next to indicators: the moment something says buy here, risk this much and get out there, it can be backtested. Silver Bullet is the first, and it still draws on the chart as before - one definition, used twice, so what you see and what you test can never drift apart

A Backtest tab that runs a strategy over the symbol and timeframe the chart is already showing. You set the starting balance, the date range, how much one trade may lose - as a percent of the account or a fixed amount - where the target sits relative to that, and a ceiling on how much the position may carry. Every strategy setting has its own field and its own explanation

A Results tab that keeps every run. Equity from zero, win rate, net profit, maximum drawdown, profit factor, expectancy, the longest winning and losing streaks, and a breakdown by direction, by session and by how each trade ended. Ctrl-click to lay several runs over each other - compared in percent, because in money the run that started richer always wins

Step through a run's trades one at a time. The chart jumps to each trade, framed on it with the bars either side, and draws it the way the position tool does: risk zone to the stop, reward zone to the target, entry, direction, reward-to-risk, and what the trade actually made

Every stored run keeps what it was run with - the market, the range, the balance, every strategy parameter and the costs it was charged - and shows them under the figures. A result without its settings cannot be compared to anything

Anything that deletes for good now asks first, and says what will be lost. The Delete key still removes a selected drawing straight away: that is deliberate enough already, and a prompt on every press would make tidying up a chart a chore

Position sizes are capped at what the account can actually carry. Risking a percent behind a tight stop asks for many times the balance, and the fees on that phantom size decided the result - a month of BTC turned 54 trades into 4,924 of fees against a 10,000 account, where the same run now pays 995
Errors are shown wherever they happen. They used to be rendered only inside the chart's data panel, so anything that went wrong elsewhere was caught, stored and shown to nobody

Silver Bullet setups, drawn end to end: liquidity is taken, the reversal tears a fair value gap, price closes past the last candle that opposed it, and the entry sits at the retest of that gap - all inside one of the three Silver Bullet hours in New York time. Entry, stop and target are drawn with it, and each setup is carried forward to whichever it reached first. A run that never comes back is a break rather than a setup and is not marked

You choose what counts: which of the three hours, whether the whole chain has to fall inside one or only the entry, how far the gap may lag the sweep and the entry the gap, the smallest gap worth trading in points or percent, and where the target sits as a multiple of the risk

Drawings now carry their own stroke: colour, a width from 1 to 4, and a solid, dashed or dotted line. Pick a drawing and the bar appears over the chart next to it; what you choose also arms the next drawing, so a style set once stays set. Fib, measure, range profile and position blocks keep their own dashes, because there the pattern means something

Hold shift while dragging to lock a drawing to one axis - level or upright. It works while drawing a new shape, while dragging one end of an existing one, and while moving a whole shape. The axis follows the direction you actually dragged further on screen, so it does not change when the price scale is zoomed

Stop hunts on the chart: levels price ran through to fill the stops resting behind them, and then closed back inside. A run that keeps going is a break, not a hunt, and is not marked — only what happens after the wick tells the two apart. Each one is drawn as three marks: how long the level sat there in plain sight, the stretch of price that only traded to fill stops, and the wait until the reclaim was confirmed

Choose what counts as liquidity: swing highs and lows, equal highs and lows (the real stop clusters, matched within a tolerance you set), the extremes of closed trading sessions — or any combination. You also set how many bars price has for the reclaim, how far the wick must clear the level, and how long the reclaim has to hold afterwards. A level is only hunted once; the stops behind it filled the first time

A range volume profile you draw yourself: pick the tool, drag across a stretch of chart, and the volume traded in it is profiled over that span. Built from the same 1-minute bars as the profile on the right, so both agree about where price actually changed hands

Trading sessions on the chart — Asia, London and New York as a futures set, the four classic centres as a forex set, or your own with a name, a time zone and a window. Each session knows the local time of its market, so when the clocks change somewhere the session moves with them instead of drifting an hour off
Every indicator setting now explains itself on hover, in the app's own style rather than a system tooltip. The text sits with the setting it describes, so a new option cannot arrive without one
The minimum size for fair value gaps reads as points as well as percent. Percent keeps its meaning as price moves; points are what you read off your own chart and size a stop in

The VWAP reset — daily or weekly — never actually happened on the chart. Bar times reached the calculation as seconds where a calendar date was expected, which put every bar in 1970 and made both anchors behave like 'whole range'

Inverted fair value gaps were nearly all missing. A retest was counted as using the zone up, when a retest is the reason it is drawn; and a zone that had been broken again was dropped from the stretch of chart where it applied. Both are corrected, and a month of BTC now shows 41 open inversions where it showed 28
The width of a fair value gap box is counted from the bars that formed the gap, so a width of 3 is three candles wide wherever the gap ends up being broken

Fair value gaps on the chart, under Add. A gap is drawn from the three bars that formed it and stays until price fills it — you decide what filling means: first touch, the midpoint, fully crossed, or a close beyond. A minimum size, a window of recent bars and a box width keep the chart as busy or as quiet as you want it

Inverted fair value gaps as a second indicator. A gap that price closes through has failed, and the same prices then read the other way round: failed support becomes resistance. Each zone is drawn from the gap it came from, and a retest leaves it standing — it ends only when price closes back through it

Both zone indicators let you pick the bullish and bearish colour yourself. The palette leads with the candle tones so a zone speaks the same up-is-light, down-is-blue language as the rest of the chart, and every choice works in light and dark

Scrolling back through history no longer stops the chart with an error about bars being out of order. On any timeframe above 1 minute, the boundary between one loaded page and the next fell inside a period, so the same bar arrived twice

The first bar of each page loaded while scrolling back was built from only part of its period, so its open, high, low and close were wrong without anything looking amiss. Pages now start and end on period boundaries

The position tool writes everything inside the block now: target and stop with their price and percentage, the entry on the reward side, and the direction with reward-to-risk against the entry line in the risk zone

The summary box above a position block is gone, along with the risk and reward amounts it showed. The percentages carry the same information and compare across instruments — and the box had been covering the target's percentage
Download years of 1-minute history straight from Binance's public archive — no API key, no account, no subscription. Every file is checksum-verified and stored on your own machine
Charts in seven timeframes, from 1 minute to daily, with older bars loading as you scroll back
Volume profile with point of control, value area and a buy/sell delta. It is always built from 1-minute bars, so the profile does not change just because you switched the chart to 4h
Indicators: moving average, exponential MA, Bollinger Bands, RSI, ATR and VWAP. Oscillators get their own pane instead of sharing a scale with price

Drawing tools — trend line, ray, horizontal and vertical line, rectangle, Fibonacci retracement and a measure tool. Drawings are anchored to time and price, so they stay put through zooming, panning and timeframe changes, and are saved per symbol

Long and short position tools showing entry, stop and target with the risk zone in red and the reward zone in green, plus risk, reward and reward-to-risk. Zone colours and fill opacity are adjustable per drawing

Backtesting engine with market, limit and stop orders, brackets that cancel each other, spread, slippage and commission. Fills are resolved through the 1-minute bars, so a bar that touches both your stop and your target is decided by what actually happened first rather than by a guess
Strategies are plain JavaScript with an onBar hook. They cannot see past the current bar, and an order never fills on the bar that placed it
Light and dark mode, or follow the system — including the native window frame
